<reason>Both sides argued with unusual discipline and the debate narrowed cleanly to one clause: whether an insurer may charge more to a driver who declines monitoring. PRO did real work getting CON to adopt most of its "fair terms" (no resale, no secondary use, no location scoring) and landed a genuine hit with the sorting-versus-behavior-change point (sorting moves money, it doesn't save lives). But CON won the remaining clause. The adverse-selection mechanism in [B2.1]-[B2.4] was the strongest causal argument in the debate and PRO never squarely neutralized it; PRO's A1 concession that the unmonitored rate may later rise on claims experience was turned by CON into "group averaging — the behavioural costume without the behaviour," which inverted PRO's own redlining charge. CON's claims-history analogy and the closing reductio of "consent that costs you money is not consent" (it would abolish all risk-based pricing) exposed that PRO's operative principle was overbroad, and the ZIP-code counterfactual gave a third-party reader a clear reason the motion's remedy leaves the nurse worse off. Both sides had clipped speeches and both answered pressure questions with proper A1/A2 labels, so execution roughly cancels. A clear but competitive CON win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B4.4]-[B4.5] seizing PRO's own A1 answer — that the refuser pool's rate may rise later on claims experience — and showing this means the nurse is ultimately priced on the average of everyone else who refused, i.e., exactly the identity averaging PRO condemned. Combined with the closing test of [A5.6], this turned PRO's central principle against itself.</best_rebuttal>
